comments.author: @rtvitko
comments.text:
Thank you for another excellent video presentation, @BecauseGeography. I enjoyed your work and wanted to raise an item important to me and many other people from this part of the world. It is apparent you only intended respect to the peoples you spoke of here. But there is an imprecision that may leave people with the wrong idea. I just do not know what the right word is, and maybe it does not exist yet. But I do not think it is accurate to identify "Polynesians" as the greatest navigators EVER....because there are no Polynesians. 

The navigators and wayfinders you mention here come from all of the people groups, not just those called "Polynesian" today. Mau Piailug was from Satawal in Micronesia and the islands he sailed among were not differentiated in his mind or his lore among Melanesia, Polynesia and Micronesia. Other navigators from other people groups in different islands do not use those groups; they just don't offer anything meaningful. Factor in the Malagasy people and their forebears, and the inaccuracy is magnified because Malagasy seem to be closer to Dayak people from Borneo and the Indonesian islands, and their amazing achievements are not "Polynesian." The terms are artificial and introduce inaccuracy because they don't map exactly to the people. 

I don't know if there is a word that covers the people you talk about. The three groups Melanesia, Micronesia and Polynesia are geographic conveniences. They are not just "Austronesian," although that term seems to cover a larger number of people. However, it leaves out the other ethnic groups that likely contributed not just with their genetic material, but with their languages, cultures, knowledge and skills. The feats of navigation you describe took place across thousands of years and across thousands of miles in distance. A vast swath of the world was touched by the people who used this navigation, and some of these people still use these skills today. As a suggestion for a future video, perhaps you might present the Marshall Islands stick charts. Sounds primitive, but far from it. A great next step after this wonderful work of the navigators.

Which brings us back to what I ask you and the community to think about and help us answer. When we say Austronesian we leave out the contributions of the former people of Sahul who became today's Papuans, Australians and Torres Strait Islanders. It does not reckon with contributions from Africa, Asia and South America. Some of those people do have more or less admixture from Austronesians. But they also have their own body of knowledge which has become part of a larger group of wayfinging lore. 

So my question is, what is the best term to describe the people who exercised a navigational theory that saw these many lands settled?

I don't know the word and do not know if the word ever existed. But you raised the point with this video. In doing homage and bringing honor to the feats of a great people, you describe them as Polynesians. I think that leaves out too much. What do you think? Where can we go from here? I don't know the words. We may need to make a word or terms to help describe this phenomenon. Any suggestions?

replies.author: @rtvitko
replies.text: Post post scriptum...maybe there is a way to use some older root word. ProtoMalayoPolynesian reconstructs "tao" to mean person and "qulun" to mean stranger. Those roots are remarkably consistent in many words used by successor languages. So maybe that can inform the thought exercise...Or "waka for canoe?

replies.author: @rtvitko
replies.text: Reclama.... or post scriptum....other suggestions include the settlement of Guam and the Marianas and Bonins, as well as the migration of the Yapese and the settlement of Palau. The Second Island Chain today, may indeed have been the second island chain pursued besides the larger First Island Chain.

comments.author: @TheKalihiMan
comments.text: Sailing against the prevailing winds was very much a deliberate choice, as it made a return voyage in the event that no land was found before supplies were depleted easier with the wind to your back and reduced the risk of being stranded in open ocean. Despite its size compared to the rest of Polynesia, New Zealand is somewhat of an outlier in that it is roughly downwind of the trade winds coming from Eastern Polynesia. The difficulty of a return voyage, combined with the abundance of resources compared to the smaller islands, might explain why contact with the rest of Polynesia was lost shortly after the initial settlement period.
